G1-233.h1: Draw the Clock Hands: O'Clock Times
G1-233.title: Draw Clock Hands to the Hour | Free Printable PDF
G1-233.metaDescription: Draw the clock hands worksheet: four empty faces and four whole hours. Long hand to the twelve, short hand to the number. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-233.p1: Every time on this Grade 1 page is a whole hour — 3:00, 7:00, 11:00 — and every clock face is empty. The child reads the digital chip under a face, then draws two hands: the long minute hand straight up to the twelve, and the short hour hand pointing squarely at the number the chip names. Four faces, four whole hours, no minutes to work out anywhere. It is the first rung of the drawing-the-hands ladder, and deliberately the plainest one on it.
G1-233.p2: Starting at o'clock isolates one idea: the two hands are not the same. Children who have only ever read clocks often draw both hands the same length, or push the hour hand right out to the rim because it looks tidier there. On this page the difference between them is the answer — a long hand to twelve and a distinctly shorter one to the hour — so it gets rehearsed a dozen times before minutes complicate anything. Ask which hand goes in first every single time; that habit is what sticks.
G1-233.p3: Print it free as a PDF and keep a spare copy for the day a child needs an easy win. Once whole hours are drawn confidently, half past clocks are the natural next step, and the mixed times page is where all the steps finally meet. Reading a clock face is the companion skill worth practising alongside it.

G1-234.h1: Draw the Clock Hands: Half Past
G1-234.title: Draw Clock Hands: Half Past | Free Printable PDF
G1-234.metaDescription: Half past worksheet: every digital chip ends in :30 and the child draws both hands. Minute hand to the six, hour hand halfway. Free Grade 1 PDF.
G1-234.p1: Every chip on this Grade 1 page reads half past — 2:30, 6:30, 9:30 — and every clock face is waiting to be filled in. The child draws the long minute hand straight down to the six, then places the short hour hand not on a number at all, but exactly between the hour just gone and the hour coming next. Four faces, all of them at :30, so the single new idea gets repeated rather than met once and lost.
G1-234.p2: This page exists because of one very stubborn mistake. Asked for half past four, most children plant the hour hand firmly on the 4, where it has always gone before, and produce a clock that reads roughly four o'clock. The hour hand moves continuously; by half past it has crawled halfway toward the next number. Drawing four of these in a row, with someone asking where the hour hand has got to each time, is what converts that idea from something heard into something the child has actually done.
G1-234.p3: The sheet prints free as a PDF, which makes it easy to hand out again a week later — this one rewards revisiting. Whole-hour clock faces are the gentler page to start from, quarter past and quarter to is where the same halfway thinking gets finer, and number words to 20 helps with reading the times themselves.

G1-235.h1: Draw the Clock Hands: Quarter Past and Quarter To
G1-235.title: Draw Clock Hands: Quarter Hours | Free Printable PDF
G1-235.metaDescription: Quarter hours worksheet: quarter past and quarter to times drawn on empty clock faces, minute hand to the three or the nine. Free Grade 1 PDF.
G1-235.p1: The four times on this Grade 1 page land on the quarters — :15 and :45, quarter past and quarter to. The child reads each digital chip and draws the minute hand out to the three or to the nine, then judges where the short hour hand has crept to: a quarter of the way past the hour, or three quarters of the way toward the next one. The faces are entirely empty, so both hands are the child's decision.
G1-235.p2: Quarter hours are where clock language starts pulling against the numbers on the chip. Quarter to eight is written 7:45, and the hour hand ends up nearly at the eight — so a child who has learned to match the spoken hour to the drawn hour hand finally meets a case where the words and the picture agree with each other but not with the digits. Drawing it settles that confusion far better than explaining it does. Say each time aloud in both forms while the pencil is still moving.
G1-235.p3: Print the PDF free; a quiet ten minutes is all it asks for. Half past clocks are the page underneath this one and five-minute times the page above it, while the mixed review is where the quarters get tested against everything else the clock can say.

G1-236.h1: Draw the Clock Hands to Five Minutes
G1-236.title: Draw Clock Hands to Five Minutes | Free Printable PDF
G1-236.metaDescription: Five-minute clock worksheet: read times like 4:25 and draw both hands on an empty face. Count the dial round in fives. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-236.p1: Times on this Grade 1 page step in fives — 1:20, 4:35, 8:55 — and every clock face starts blank. To place the minute hand the child counts round the dial in fives, five for the one, ten for the two, fifteen for the three, until the count reaches the number the chip asks for. Then the short hour hand goes in, somewhere between two numerals rather than on one. Four faces, four five-minute times, and a lot of counting round the rim.
G1-236.p2: This is the page where the clock face stops being a ring of hour numbers and becomes two scales at once. The 5 on the dial means five o'clock to one hand and twenty-five minutes to the other, and nobody reads a real clock until that double duty feels ordinary. Counting the dial aloud in fives while drawing is the whole method, and it doubles as skip-counting practice that pays off in multiplication later. Expect the counting to be slow at first and noticeably quicker by the fourth face.
G1-236.p3: The worksheet prints free as a PDF, so a second copy costs nothing when the counting needs another run. Quarter hours make a gentler stop on the way here, mixed times are the natural page afterwards, and Grade 2 telling time carries the same five-minute reading into next year.

G1-237.h1: Draw the Clock Hands: Mixed Times Review
G1-237.title: Draw Clock Hands: Mixed Times | Free Printable PDF
G1-237.metaDescription: Mixed clock times worksheet: whole hours, half past, quarter hours and five-minute times together on four empty faces. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-237.p1: This Grade 1 page mixes everything the clock has offered so far. One chip might read 6:00, the next 2:30, the one after 9:45 or 3:20 — so the child never settles into a single routine, because every face asks a slightly different question. They read the digital time, work out where the minute hand belongs, and then place the short hour hand accordingly: on a number, halfway between two, or somewhere in between the two.
G1-237.p2: Mixing the times is what turns practice into a check. On a page where every clock says half past, a child can succeed without ever really reading the chip; here they cannot. Interleaving the four cases forces a decision before every stroke, which is harder and far more informative — an adult can see at a glance whether the hour hand is still being parked on numerals, or whether the fives are being counted or merely guessed. It works well as a Friday page, or as a quick check before Grade 2 time work begins.
G1-237.p3: Print it free as a PDF and keep the finished sheets; two of them a month apart make progress visible. If one case wobbles, the single-focus pages are still there — whole hours, half past, quarter hours, five minutes — and reading a clock face rounds out the same skill from the other direction.

G1-238.title: Addition Word Problems Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-238.metaDescription: Addition word problems with fruit pictures: two stories, a picture strip to count and a dot-grid work space. Free printable Grade 1 math PDF.
G1-238.p1: Every story on this Grade 1 page adds. Someone picks a few apples and then picks a few more; someone brings pears to the table and a friend brings some too. Under each story sits a strip of fruit pictures showing exactly what the words describe, and beside it a dot-grid panel for working. The child reads, counts the fruit if they need to, jots or draws on the grid, and writes the total in the answer box.
G1-238.p2: Keeping every story on this page an addition story is a deliberate simplification. A word problem asks a child to do two hard things at once — decide what is happening, then compute — and beginners often fail at the first while being perfectly capable of the second. With the operation fixed, all the attention goes to modelling the story: who had what, what arrived, what the question actually wants. Addition also turns up in more than one shape here, joining and putting together, which is worth naming aloud while the pictures are still in front of them.
G1-238.p3: The page prints free as a PDF, and it reads aloud beautifully for children still building fluency. Subtraction stories are the obvious companion sheet, the mixed picture word problems put the two operations back together, and mental math within 20 keeps the totals quick.

G1-239.title: Subtraction Word Problems Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-239.metaDescription: Subtraction word problems with fruit pictures: two take-away stories with picture support and a dot-grid work space. Free printable Grade 1 PDF.
G1-239.p1: Both stories on this Grade 1 page take something away. A basket of oranges loses a few to a hungry family; a plate of strawberries is shared out and some get eaten. A picture strip underneath restates the situation in fruit icons the child can count and cross off, and a dot-grid panel gives room to work. They read the story, lean on the pictures as much as they like, and write what is left in the answer box.
G1-239.p2: Subtraction stories are quietly harder than they look, because taking away is only one of their shapes. The same minus sign covers what is left over, how many more one person has than another, and how many are missing — and children who learn the shortcut of grabbing the two numbers and subtracting the smaller from the larger get away with it for a while, then abruptly stop getting away with it. Picture support is the antidote: it is difficult to misread a story you can physically count and cross out.
G1-239.p3: Print the PDF free and ask the child to point at what disappeared before they write anything down. Addition stories make the natural pairing, fact family houses show why the two operations are really one relationship, and word problems within 10 is the gentler edition when the reading still feels heavy.

G1-240.h1: Word Problems Within 10: Small Numbers, Real Stories
G1-240.title: Word Problems Within 10 | Free Printable PDF
G1-240.metaDescription: Word problems within 10 for Grade 1: short picture stories with totals no higher than ten, plus a dot-grid work space. Free printable math PDF.
G1-240.p1: Every number on this Grade 1 page stays inside ten. The stories still add and subtract, still come with a strip of fruit pictures and a dot-grid panel to work on, but nothing ever climbs past a total the child can hold on two hands. Read the story, count the pictures, work it out on the grid, write the answer in the box — with the arithmetic small enough that nobody gets lost halfway through a sentence.
G1-240.p2: Small numbers here are a reading decision rather than a mathematical one. A first grader working through an unfamiliar sentence is already spending most of their attention on the words; if the calculation waiting at the end is also demanding, the whole thing collapses and the child quietly concludes they are bad at word problems. Keeping every total within ten frees that attention for comprehension, which is the part actually being taught. That makes this a good page for children new to the language of the classroom, and a good first page of the year for everyone else.
G1-240.p3: It prints free as a PDF and works well read aloud in pairs, one child reading while the other solves. When the reading feels easy, addition stories and subtraction stories raise the numbers, and the compact three-story page is the next step up in stamina.

G1-241.h1: Word Problem Practice: Three Stories on One Page
G1-241.title: Grade 1 Word Problem Practice | Free Printable PDF
G1-241.metaDescription: Word problem practice for Grade 1: three compact picture stories on one page, mixing addition and subtraction, each with an answer box. Free PDF.
G1-241.p1: Three stories fit on this Grade 1 page instead of the usual two, each trimmed a little to keep everything readable — a short story, a picture strip, a smaller work space, an answer box. The mix adds and subtracts, so every story opens with a decision before any counting starts. It is the same task the other word problem pages set, packed slightly tighter and asked one more time.
G1-241.p2: Three problems in a row is a small test of endurance, and endurance matters more in word problems than in any other kind of arithmetic. A child who solves the first story carefully, the second hastily and the third by guessing is telling you something useful, and it is not that they cannot subtract. Because the layout is compact and the instructions never change, this page also runs well as homework or as an early-finisher sheet — nobody needs it explained twice, and it can be marked in under a minute.
G1-241.p3: Print the PDF free, and consider timing nothing at all: careful beats quick at this stage. Addition stories and subtraction stories are the single-operation pages to fall back on, while animal word problems tell the same kind of story with a completely different picture bank.

G1-213@animals.title: Animal Word Problems Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-213@animals.metaDescription: Animal word problems for Grade 1: two picture stories about ducks, rabbits and friends, with counting icons and a dot-grid work space. Free PDF.
G1-213@animals.p1: This Grade 1 word problems page runs on animals. Two short stories — ducks arriving at a pond, rabbits disappearing into the grass, a farmer counting sheep — sit above a strip of animal pictures showing exactly what the words describe, plus a dot-grid panel for working out. The child reads, counts the animals if that helps, and writes the answer in the box. The mathematics matches the fruit edition exactly; only the cast has changed.
G1-213@animals.p2: Changing the pictures is not decoration. Children who meet the same story structure only ever with apples can quietly conclude that the method belongs to apples, and then stumble the first time a problem is about ducks. Re-running identical structures across different nouns is how a strategy becomes portable — and animals happen to carry more story with them, which loosens up the retelling that is such a good check on understanding. The vocabulary is a bonus for children still building the everyday nouns of their school language.
G1-213@animals.p3: The sheet prints free as a PDF, and animals invite a good follow-up: make up one more story about the same picture. The fruit edition of these picture word problems is the sibling to run alongside it, and word problems within 10 keeps the numbers small while the reading grows.

G2-255.title: 2-Digit Column Addition | Free Printable PDF
G2-255.metaDescription: 2-digit column addition worksheet without regrouping: six stacked sums with place-value boxes, starting at the ones. Free printable Grade 2 PDF.
G2-255.p1: Six two-digit additions stand in columns down this Grade 2 page, each digit in its own place-value box: 34 + 25, 61 + 17, and four more of the same shape. No column ever totals more than nine, so nothing is ever carried anywhere on the sheet. The child adds the ones, writes that digit in its box, moves left, adds the tens, and writes that one — the same four moves, six times over.
G2-255.p2: The habit being built here is physical as much as mathematical. Start at the right, work one column at a time, keep one digit per box, and never let the pencil drift leftwards before the ones are finished. Left to right feels natural to a child who reads that way, and it works perfectly well until the first carry, at which point it stops working at all — so the direction is worth insisting on now, while insisting costs nothing. The boxes do quiet work too: crooked columns cause more early errors than faulty adding does.
G2-255.p3: The page prints free as a PDF and suits a short daily run more than a long weekly one. Two-digit column subtraction is the matching sheet, three-digit column addition widens the same routine, and addition with carrying is where this method finally earns its keep.

G2-256.title: 2-Digit Column Subtraction | Free Printable PDF
G2-256.metaDescription: 2-digit column subtraction worksheet without borrowing: six stacked problems with place-value boxes, start with the ones. Free Grade 2 math PDF.
G2-256.p1: Six two-digit subtractions run down this Grade 2 page in columns, ones under ones and tens under tens: 68 − 24, 95 − 51, and four more built the same way. In every problem the top digit is the larger one in both columns, so nothing is ever borrowed. The child subtracts the ones, writes the digit in its box, moves across to the tens, and does exactly the same thing again.
G2-256.p2: This is the right moment to name a habit that will cause trouble later. Because the top digit is always the bigger one here, a child can answer every problem correctly while believing the rule is take the small one from the big one — and that belief survives happily until the first problem where it is wrong. Say out loud, on this easy page, that we take the bottom number from the top one, and that a case is coming where the top is too small and something will have to be exchanged. Groundwork laid now saves a difficult week later on.
G2-256.p3: Print it free as a PDF for regular short practice. Two-digit column addition is the partner sheet, the column method review interleaves both operations, and subtraction with borrowing is the step this page is quietly preparing the ground for.

G2-257.h1: 3-Digit Numbers in Columns: Add and Subtract
G2-257.title: 3-Digit Column Add & Subtract | Free Printable PDF
G2-257.metaDescription: 3-digit column arithmetic without regrouping: six mixed addition and subtraction problems with hundreds, tens and ones boxes. Free Grade 2 PDF.
G2-257.p1: Three columns now — hundreds, tens and ones — and the six problems on this Grade 2 page mix addition with subtraction, so the sign has to be read before anything else happens: 342 + 215 sits beside 687 − 143. There is no carrying and no borrowing anywhere on the page. The child checks the sign, starts at the ones, and works leftward through all three places, one digit per box.
G2-257.p2: Mixing the two operations changes what the page is really testing. On a sheet of pure additions the sign becomes wallpaper and children stop looking at it; here the very first move is a decision, and the classic error is a subtraction carried out as an addition simply because the previous problem was one. Pausing to read the sign aloud before the pencil moves is a habit worth a fortnight of nagging. It is also the habit that makes mixed test papers survivable in the years ahead.
G2-257.p3: The worksheet prints free as a PDF and makes a solid mid-week check, since it takes only a few minutes to mark. Two-digit column addition and two-digit column subtraction are the narrower pages behind it, three-digit column addition keeps the width without the switching, and the column method review is the fuller mixed set to reach for once three digits stop feeling new.

G2-258.title: 3-Digit Column Addition | Free Printable PDF
G2-258.metaDescription: 3-digit column addition worksheet without carrying: six stacked sums into the hundreds, each with place-value boxes. Free printable Grade 2 PDF.
G2-258.p1: Six additions into the hundreds fill this Grade 2 page — 415 + 132, 623 + 254 and their like — each stacked in place-value boxes three columns wide. Every column adds to nine or less, so no carrying is needed anywhere on the sheet. Ones first, then tens, then hundreds, one digit written into each box as the child works steadily leftward.
G2-258.p2: The useful discovery on this page is that a third column adds no new mathematics whatsoever. A child who can run the routine over two places runs it over three by doing exactly the same thing once more, and noticing that is worth more than the six answers are. It is also where place value gets a workout: the 4 in 415 is four hundreds, and the column it sits in is the only reason the digit means that. Bigger numbers, identical method, is a genuinely encouraging thing for a seven-year-old to find out.
G2-258.p3: Print the PDF free — one a week is plenty at this width, and the answers can be checked in a minute. Two-digit column addition is the shorter version to warm up on, the three-digit mixed page drops subtraction into the same layout, and three-digit addition with carrying is where the hundreds finally start to bite.

G2-259.h1: Column Method Review: Mixed Widths and Operations
G2-259.title: Column Method Review Grade 2 | Free Printable PDF
G2-259.metaDescription: Column method review for Grade 2: six problems mixing 2-digit and 3-digit addition and subtraction, still without regrouping. Free printable PDF.
G2-259.p1: This Grade 2 review page shuffles everything the column method has covered so far. Two-digit problems sit beside three-digit ones, additions beside subtractions, and all six are still free of carrying and borrowing. Nothing on the page is new; what is new is that no two problems in a row necessarily ask the same thing, so each one has to be read properly before the child starts at the ones column.
G2-259.p2: A review like this is best used as a gate. Regrouping is genuinely difficult, and it goes badly for children whose underlying routine is still shaky — every carried digit lands on top of an existing wobble. Six mixed problems answered accurately, with no prompting about where to start or which way to work, is a fair sign that the method itself is secure and the next difficulty can safely be added. Six problems with two careless slips is a sign to spend another week here instead, which is not a setback at all.
G2-259.p3: The sheet prints free as a PDF and doubles neatly as a short assessment. The single-focus pages behind it — two-digit addition, two-digit subtraction, three-digit addition — are still there for anything that wobbles, and addition and subtraction with regrouping is what this page is clearing the way for.

G2-260.title: Reading Measuring Jugs in ml | Free Printable PDF
G2-260.metaDescription: Measuring jugs worksheet: six jugs filled to different levels, read each scale and write the amount in milliliters. Free printable Grade 2 PDF.
G2-260.p1: Six measuring jugs, and nothing else, fill this Grade 2 page. Each one holds liquid to a different level, and each carries a scale with labelled marks and unlabelled ticks in between them. The child works out what a single tick is worth, follows the surface of the liquid to the nearest line, and writes the amount in milliliters underneath. Six readings, one unit, and no balance scales competing for attention.
G2-260.p2: Giving capacity a page of its own lets one method be taught properly. Look at two labelled marks, count how many gaps lie between them, divide — now every tick has a value and the jug can be read rather than guessed at. Children who skip that step write down the number nearest the liquid and are routinely fifty milliliters out. It pairs beautifully with a real jug at the sink: pour to a line, predict the reading, then check. Ten minutes of that makes the printed jugs look obvious.
G2-260.p3: The page prints free as a PDF, and a spare copy is handy for the child who wants to check a real measuring cup against it. Balance scales in grams is the mass half of the same skill, the jugs to 2000 ml page takes the numbers higher, and the combined capacity and mass sheet puts jugs and scales back on one page.

G2-261.h1: Balance Scales in Grams: Read the Mass
G2-261.title: Balance Scales in Grams | Free Printable PDF
G2-261.metaDescription: Balance scales worksheet: six pan balances with a vehicle on one side and gram weights on the other. Add the weights, write the mass. Free PDF.
G2-261.p1: Six balance scales share this Grade 2 page, and a little vehicle sits on one pan of each — a truck, a bus, a tractor — with gram weights stacked on the other pan until the two sides level out. The child adds up the weights and writes the vehicle's mass in grams underneath. No jugs here and no milliliters: six balances and a single unit for the whole page.
G2-261.p2: A pan balance teaches something a bathroom scale never can. It does not display a number; it makes a statement — these two sides are equal — and the child has to add the known weights in order to discover the unknown one. That is an equation in physical form, and it is the same idea that later turns into the missing number in 40 + ☐ = 65. It also makes mass concrete in a way that pictures of dials do not: 500 grams becomes a thing you would feel in your hand rather than a label to copy out.
G2-261.p3: Print it free as a PDF and, if there is a balance in the school cupboard, weigh something real afterwards — nothing beats the actual object. Measuring jugs in milliliters is the capacity twin, the mixed page with fine 50 ml marks sharpens the reading further, and column addition keeps the adding of weights quick.

G2-262.h1: Reading Scales in Small Steps: 50 ml Marks
G2-262.title: Reading Scales in 50 ml Steps | Free Printable PDF
G2-262.metaDescription: Fine-scale measurement worksheet: jugs and balances marked in small 50 ml steps, so readings land between the labelled numbers. Free Grade 2 PDF.
G2-262.p1: The jugs and balances on this Grade 2 page are marked far more finely than usual: the ticks step in fifties, so a reading of 250 ml or 350 ml sits between the labelled hundreds rather than on one of them. Vehicles ride the balance pans as before. The child still reads each scale and writes the amount with its unit, but now the answer often lands on an unlabelled line and has to be worked out rather than simply seen.
G2-262.p2: Fine scales are where scale reading turns into a real skill. Shown a level halfway between 200 and 300, a child who has only ever met labelled marks writes 200, or 300, or occasionally 250 by lucky guess. Counting the gaps, dividing, and naming the tick value is the method that survives every scale they will ever meet — thermometers, rulers, measuring spoons, the pointer on a kitchen dial. It rewards slowing down, which is precisely what measurement work should be teaching at this age.
G2-262.p3: The worksheet prints free as a PDF, and it is worth reading one jug together aloud before letting the child loose on the rest. The plain measuring jugs page is the gentler starting point, balance scales in grams isolates the mass side, and the big jugs to 2000 ml take the same careful reading up into larger numbers.

G2-263.h1: Measuring Jugs to 2000 ml: Reading Bigger Scales
G2-263.title: Measuring Jugs to 2000 ml | Free Printable PDF
G2-263.metaDescription: Big measuring jugs worksheet: six large jugs scaled up to 2000 ml, read each liquid level and write the amount in milliliters. Free Grade 2 PDF.
G2-263.p1: The jugs on this Grade 2 page are the big ones, scaled all the way to 2000 ml, and the six readings run into the hundreds and thousands rather than the tens. Each jug shows labelled marks with ticks between them, and the child works out the tick value, reads the liquid level, and writes the amount in milliliters. Exactly the same method as the small jugs; considerably larger numbers to write down.
G2-263.p2: Working up to 2000 ml is where capacity starts connecting to the world outside the page. A liter is a carton of milk, two liters is the big bottle of water, and 1500 ml is neither of those but sits sensibly between them — and that sense of size is exactly what is missing when a child cheerfully writes 30 ml for a bucket. Estimating before reading is the habit to build here: look at the jug, guess, then read and compare. Being wrong by a little and noticing it is worth more than being right by accident.
G2-263.p3: It prints free as a PDF and goes well with a two-liter bottle standing on the table for comparison. The standard measuring jugs page is the smaller-numbers version, the 50 ml step page trains the finer reading, and capacity and mass together brings the balance scales back alongside.

G2-252@animals.h1: Capacity and Mass with Animals: Jugs and Scales
G2-252@animals.title: Capacity and Mass with Animals | Free Printable PDF
G2-252@animals.metaDescription: Animal measurement worksheet: three jugs to read in milliliters and three balance scales weighing animals in grams. Free printable Grade 2 PDF.
G2-252@animals.p1: This Grade 2 measurement page splits itself between capacity and mass, with animals sitting on the balance pans. Three measuring jugs hold liquid at different levels for the child to read in milliliters; three balances weigh a duck, a hedgehog, a cat against gram weights for the child to read in grams. Six readings altogether, each one written down together with its unit.
G2-252@animals.p2: Animals on the pans invite a question that a page of boxes never does: which one is heavier, and by how much? That single follow-up turns a reading exercise into comparison, subtraction and a small science conversation — how heavy might a real hedgehog be, is a duck heavier than a cat, would any of them actually sit still on a school balance. Measurement lives in that talk at least as much as in the writing down, and a themed page gives a class something to argue about while the units and tick marks quietly do their work.
G2-252@animals.p3: Print the PDF free and keep the comparison questions coming after the last box is filled. The vehicles edition of capacity and mass is the sibling sheet, reading measuring jugs isolates the capacity half, and balance scales in grams does the same for mass.

G2-264.h1: Easy Symmetry Drawing: First Mirror Pictures
G2-264.title: Easy Symmetry Drawing Grade 2 | Free Printable PDF
G2-264.metaDescription: Easy symmetry worksheet: four small pixel-grid pictures, half drawn, to mirror across the coral line square by square. Free printable Grade 2 PDF.
G2-264.p1: The four pictures on this Grade 2 page are the small, forgiving ones: a handful of colored squares each, sitting close to the coral mirror line down the middle. Half of every picture is already drawn; the child colors the missing half, square by square, until the two sides match. Short distances from the line and simple outlines make this the gentlest page in the whole symmetry set.
G2-264.p2: Easy figures deserve a page of their own because they let the method be taught rather than merely survived. Put a finger on a colored square, count the steps sideways to the line, count the same number of steps out the other side, color it in. On a small figure that count is one or two, so the routine is learned before it has to carry any weight — and a child who finishes four pictures that genuinely look right arrives at the harder sheet believing they can do this, which matters more than most of the geometry does.
G2-264.p3: The page prints free as a PDF and the finished pictures are cheerful enough to keep. Hard symmetry drawing is the step up once the counting flows, mirror pictures of hearts and butterflies dress the same skill in recognisable shapes, and color by code offers more of this careful coloring.

G2-265.h1: Hard Symmetry Drawing: Bigger Mirror Pictures
G2-265.title: Hard Symmetry Drawing Grade 2 | Free Printable PDF
G2-265.metaDescription: Challenging symmetry worksheet: four detailed pixel-grid figures to complete across the mirror line, with squares far from the axis. Free Grade 2 PDF.
G2-265.p1: The four figures on this Grade 2 page carry many more squares than the easy set, and plenty of them sit well away from the coral mirror line. Half of each picture is given; the child completes the other half square by square. Longer counts, more colors to keep track of, and figures whose edges step in and out instead of running straight down the grid.
G2-265.p2: Once a figure holds thirty squares, guesswork collapses and a system is needed. The reliable one is to work a row at a time: take one row, count each colored square's distance from the line, mark its partner, finish the row, and only then move down. Children who instead hop about the picture coloring whatever catches the eye lose their place and end up with a half that is nearly right, which in symmetry is simply wrong. Learning to be systematic on a picture is a lesson that transfers a long way beyond geometry.
G2-265.p3: Print it free as a PDF, and let a checking pass be part of the job — folding the page along the line settles any dispute. Easy symmetry drawing is the sheet to drop back to if the counting slips, and the horizontal mirror line page is the genuinely tricky variant to try next.

G2-266.h1: Mirror Pictures: Heart, Butterfly, Snowman, Tree
G2-266.title: Mirror Pictures: Heart & Butterfly | Free Printable PDF
G2-266.metaDescription: Symmetry picture worksheet: complete a heart, a butterfly, a snowman and a tree on the pixel grid across the mirror line. Free printable Grade 2 PDF.
G2-266.p1: Four recognisable pictures wait half-finished on this Grade 2 page: a heart, a butterfly, a snowman and a tree, each drawn in colored squares on a grid with the coral mirror line down the middle. The child completes the missing half of every one, square by square. Because the shapes are familiar, the child knows what the picture is supposed to become long before it actually becomes it.
G2-266.p2: A named picture checks itself. A butterfly with one fat wing and one thin one looks wrong immediately, even to a child who has not yet spotted which square went astray — so the drawing becomes its own feedback and errors get found without anyone pointing at them. These four also make the natural point that symmetry is not a school invention: butterflies and trees and the human face are built this way, and once children start looking they find mirror lines everywhere between the classroom and home.
G2-266.p3: The sheet prints free as a PDF and the results are worth pinning up, four to a wall in a row. Mirror pictures of a house and crown are the man-made counterpart to these, easy symmetry drawing is the simpler warm-up for a child who is still counting slowly, and the horizontal mirror line page turns the whole idea on its side.

G2-267.h1: Mirror Pictures: House, Crown, Mushroom, Apple
G2-267.title: Mirror Pictures: House & Crown | Free Printable PDF
G2-267.metaDescription: Symmetry worksheet with four objects: house, crown, mushroom and apple, half drawn on a pixel grid to mirror square by square. Free Grade 2 PDF.
G2-267.p1: A house, a crown, a mushroom and an apple sit half-drawn on this Grade 2 page, each built from colored squares on either side of a coral mirror line. The child completes the missing half of every picture, counting each square out from the line. The crown's points and the roof of the house make for edges that step in and out, so the counting has to stay honest the whole way up.
G2-267.p2: Where the heart-and-butterfly set borrows its shapes from nature, this one borrows from design, and the distinction is worth mentioning aloud: people build things symmetrically on purpose, because balanced things look right and often work better. Houses, crowns, plates, chairs and letters are all drawn to a mirror line by choice. The stepped diagonals of a roof or a crown point are also the hardest thing on the page technically — every step has to be matched exactly, and a single square slipped shows up as a lopsided castle.
G2-267.p3: It prints free as a PDF and finishes nicely with crayons rather than pencils. The heart and butterfly set is the natural companion page, hard symmetry drawing raises the square count, and drawing the clock hands asks for the same steady, careful hand.

G2-268.h1: Mirror Below the Line: Horizontal Symmetry
G2-268.title: Symmetry: Mirror Below the Line | Free Printable PDF
G2-268.metaDescription: Horizontal symmetry worksheet: the mirror line runs across the page and the child colors below it — rocket, arrow, ice cream and robot. Free PDF.
G2-268.p1: The mirror line on this Grade 2 page runs across the page instead of down it, and the four figures — a rocket, an arrow, an ice cream and a robot, all drawn lying on their side — are complete above the line and empty below. The child mirrors each one downward, square by square: a square three rows above the line is copied three rows below, so up and down swap places while left and right stay exactly where they were.
G2-268.p2: This page exists to break a rule children invent for themselves. After a few vertical-line sheets, most of them conclude that symmetry means the left side matches the right — and then a horizontal axis arrives and their rule produces nonsense. Reflecting downward is also perceptually harder: our eyes compare side by side far more comfortably than they compare top to bottom, so counting has to take over from looking. Expect this sheet to take longer than the others, and treat that as the point of it rather than a problem with it.
G2-268.p3: Print the PDF free, and rotate the page a quarter turn if a child gets truly stuck — the familiar left-right view often unlocks it. Easy symmetry drawing and hard symmetry drawing are the vertical-line pages behind this one, and the complete-the-mirror-picture sheet is where the whole family begins.
